# Abhayarājakumāra Sutta (MN 58 (PTS MN i 392))
**ID:** MN 58 (PTS MN i 392)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Abhayarājakumāra Sutta* (MN 58) is set at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels' Sanctuary [Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995]. The Jain leader Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta (Mahāvīra) incites his follower Prince Abhaya, a son of King Bimbisāra of Magadha, to confront the Buddha with a "two-horned question" or dilemma intended to discredit him [Law 1931; Holder 2006; McTighe 2001; Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995; SuttaCentral]. Abhaya is prompted to ask whether the Buddha would ever utter words that are unwelcome and disagreeable to others: if he answers yes, he is no better than an ordinary person; if he answers no, Abhaya can point to the Buddha's harsh condemnation of Devadatta [Law 1931; Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995]. Using the pedagogical method of counter-questioning (*paṭipucchā*) [Le 2018], the Buddha circumvents the dilemma by asking Abhaya whether he would extract a foreign object or stick from his choking child's throat even if it caused pain and bleeding [Edelglass & Garfield 2009; Le 2018].
Drawing on this analogy of compassion, the Buddha articulates his criteria for speech, classifying statements across three dimensions: truth-value, pragmatic benefit (utility), and whether they are pleasant or disagreeable to the listener [Kalupahana 1992; Hayes 2003; Rogell 2003]. The Buddha explains that he will only utter speech that is factual and beneficial, knowing the opportune time to speak out of compassion for beings, regardless of whether the words are pleasing or displeasing [Edelglass & Garfield 2009; Kalupahana 1992; Hayes 2003; McTighe 2001; Rogell 2003]. Consequently, MN 58 is frequently analyzed in modern scholarship for early Buddhist perspectives on right speech, harmlessness, and the pragmatic criteria of truth [Collender 2000; Edelglass & Garfield 2009; Kalupahana 1992; Goodwin 2012].
SuttaCentral notes Chinese parallels to the sutta preserved in the *Dà zhìdù lùn* (Taishō 1509.35) and the *Śāriputrābhidharmaśāstra* (Taishō 1521.11) [SuttaCentral]. DharmaNexus reports widespread Pali-internal text reuse across 100 texts, showing substantial shared segments with the Vinaya *Khandhakas* (Kd 6, Kd 16, Kd 1), the *Gāmaṇi Saṁyutta* (SN 42), the *Aṭṭhakanipāta* (AN 8), the *Catukkanipāta* (AN 4), the *Mahāparinibbāna Sutta* (DN 16), the *Upāli Sutta* (MN 56), and the *Bodhirājakumāra Sutta* (MN 85) [DharmaNexus]. Furthermore, DharmaNexus identifies cross-language text-reuse alignments with the Tibetan *Vinayavastu* (D0001-2) and Chinese Āgama collections such as the *Saṁyuktāgama* (T 99) and *Madhyamāgama* (T 26) [DharmaNexus].
